population_estimates.note: Peninsular India under Vijayanagara hegemony; estimates from Subbarayalu and Stein.
Pre-Talikota population; Hampi alone reported at 500,000 by Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes.

description: South Indian Hindu empire (1336–1565) founded by Harihara I and Bukka Raya of the Sangama dynasty in the Deccan, in part as a defensive response to the Delhi Sultanate's southward expansion under the Tughluqs; from its capital at Vijayanagara on the Tungabhadra River (modern Hampi) the empire dominated peninsular India south of the Krishna for two-and-a-quarter centuries, controlling the trans-peninsular trade routes between the Coromandel and Malabar coasts, the maritime gold and gem trades through Mangalore and the Tamil ports, and the largest standing army on the subcontinent; the empire fought repeated wars with the Bahmani Sultanate and its Deccan successor states, sponsored a Sanskrit and Telugu literary revival, and reached its territorial and cultural peak under Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529) before being shattered at the Battle of Talikota (1565) by a coalition of Deccan sultanates that sacked Hampi.

temporal.notes: Founded by the Sangama brothers under Harihara I and Bukka Raya; capital Vijayanagara (Hampi). Fell at Talikota 1565; beyond atlas's 1500 horizon.

lifecycle_phases.description: Sangama dynasty founded by Harihara I and Bukka Raya; capital established at Vijayanagara on the Tungabhadra; first wars with Bahmani Sultanate; consolidation of the Deccan plateau south of the Krishna.
Sangama and Saluva dynasties extend imperial control to the Tamil country and Kerala coast; tributary relations with Sri Lanka; literary patronage of Sanskrit and Telugu courts.

Krishnadevaraya of the Tuluva dynasty defeats the Gajapatis of Odisha, captures Raichur (1520) from the Bijapur Sultanate, and presides over the empire's territorial maximum; Hampi flowers as one of the largest cities in the world.
